report:
## Conclusion

There is **some promising but limited evidence** that acupuncture may reduce depression symptoms during pregnancy; it is not strong enough to establish acupuncture as a proven stand-alone treatment.

The key evidence is a 2010 randomized controlled trial of 150 pregnant people with major depression. It compared depression-specific acupuncture with control acupuncture and massage. Depression-specific acupuncture produced a greater symptom reduction than the combined controls; 63% met the study’s response threshold, versus 44% in controls. This supports the view that a targeted acupuncture protocol *may* help. However, the control was not a fully inert sham, participants and practitioners could not be fully blinded, and the study was modest in size—limitations that can inflate apparent effects.  
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx

An earlier pilot randomized trial concluded only that acupuncture “holds promise,” underscoring that the evidence base began small and requires replication.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15546651/

Evidence from postpartum depression also tempers the conclusion: a small sham-controlled pilot found both electroacupuncture and sham acupuncture improved symptoms, which is consistent with non-specific effects such as expectation, attention, or the treatment setting contributing to benefit.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165032712002546

**Practical takeaway:** Acupuncture could be considered an *adjunct* if it is wanted, provided it is delivered by a qualified prenatal practitioner and coordinated with obstetric and mental-health care. It should not delay effective care for moderate-to-severe depression, suicidality, psychosis, or bipolar symptoms. ACOG identifies psychotherapy, antidepressant medication, or both as established treatment options during pregnancy.  
https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/depression-during-pregnancy
